INTRODUCTION TO BACKEND DEVELOPMENT

Frontend and Backend

Two responsibilities work together to deliver a web application.

USER INTERFACE

Frontend

What the user sees and interacts with.

  • Present content, layout and visual feedback.
  • Respond to clicks, typing and navigation.
  • Send requests and display returned results.
SERVER-SIDE LOGIC

Backend

How the service processes work and data.

  • Validate input and enforce permissions.
  • Apply application rules and access data.
  • Return results or explain failures.
Interface and interaction⇄Requests and responses⇄Application logic and data

A general model: a client requests a service, and a server provides it.

Client

Initiates requests.
A desktop app, mobile app or browser.

REQUEST →
← RESPONSE

Server

Performs work and returns a result.

SOFTWARE

A server process is a running program that listens for requests and provides a service.

Client and server describe roles. They may run on separate machines or on the same computer.

Understanding a URL

A Uniform Resource Locator tells software where and how to access a resource.

https://market.example:443/api/history?id=AAPL&range=1Y
PartMeaningExample
SchemeHow to access ithttps
HostDestination hostname or IP addressmarket.example
PortService endpoint on that host443 · default for HTTPS
PathResource / route within the service/api/history
QueryNamed options after ?id=AAPL&range=1Y

Illustrative public URL. The default port can be omitted. A #fragment is interpreted by the browser and is not sent in the HTTP request target.

Backend Development / Part 0213 / 50
PART 02 · FROM CLIENT TO SERVER

HTTP and HTTPS

HTTPS protects HTTP communication using Transport Layer Security (TLS).

HTTP

Application messages

Defines requests, responses, methods, headers and representations.

Illustrative URL
http://market.example/api/history
HTTPS

Protected communication

Uses TLS for confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.

Illustrative URL
https://market.example/api/history
HTTP · Hypertext Transfer Protocol

An application-layer protocol through which clients send requests and servers return responses.

Key features of HTTP

  • Request–response: A client sends a request; the server returns a response.
  • Stateless: HTTP does not automatically remember a user between requests. Cookies and sessions add continuity.
  • Multiple content types: Message bodies can carry HTML, JSON, images, audio, video and other files.
  • Extensible headers: Headers describe the content and carry extra information, such as cookies or authentication credentials.
Backend Development / Part 0214 / 50
PART 02 · FROM CLIENT TO SERVER

Anatomy of an HTTP Request

An HTTP/1.1 request has a request line, headers, a separating blank line and an optional body.

HTTP/1.1 example · actual watchlist endpoint
PUT /api/watchlist HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8788
Accept: application/json
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 32

{"id":"AAPL:XNAS","market":"US"}
PartWhat it contains
1. Request lineThe method, target (path + query) and HTTP version.
2. Request headersName–value fields: destination, accepted response formats, body format and size, cookies, etc.
3. Blank lineMarks the end of the headers.
4. Request bodyOptional data sent to the server: JSON, form fields, files or text.

Here, the request body is JSON identifying the stock to save. Query parameters belong to the request target, not the body.

Backend Development / Part 0215 / 50
PART 02 · FROM CLIENT TO SERVER

Anatomy of an HTTP Response

An HTTP/1.1 response has a status line, headers, a separating blank line and, when allowed, a body.

HTTP/1.1 example · illustrative stock response
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 29

{"symbol":"AAPL","price":190}
PartWhat it contains
1. Status lineThe HTTP version, status code and a reason phrase, such as 200 OK.
2. Response headersMetadata such as the body format, body size or cookies to store.
3. Blank lineMarks the end of the headers.
4. Response bodyReturned content: JSON, HTML, an image, a file, etc. Some responses, such as 204, have no body.

The body here is JSON text. Content-Type identifies its format; Content-Length gives the response body length in bytes, excluding the status line and headers. Error responses can also contain JSON.

Backend Development / Part 0218 / 50
PART 02 · FROM CLIENT TO SERVER

HTTP Status Codes

Use the status to distinguish success, redirection and different kinds of failure.

FamilyMeaningUseful examples
2xxSuccess200 OK · 201 Created · 204 No Content
3xxRedirection / related cache handling301 redirect · 304 Not Modified
4xxRequest cannot be fulfilled as sent400 invalid · 401 unauthenticated · 403 forbidden · 404 missing
5xxServer-side failure500 internal error · 502 upstream failure · 504 timeout

Common 4xx responses

  • 400 Bad Request: Invalid syntax or request data.
  • 401 Unauthorized: Missing or invalid authentication.
  • 403 Forbidden: The request is understood, but access is refused.
  • 404 Not Found: The requested resource was not found.
  • 405 Method Not Allowed: This method is not allowed for the target.
  • 429 Too Many Requests: A request-rate limit was exceeded.

HTTP outcome vs. useful data

  • 200 can still return an empty result.
  • Inspect the response body as well as the status.
Backend Development / Part 0219 / 50
PART 02 · FROM CLIENT TO SERVER

How Cookies Work

A cookie is a small name–value pair stored by the browser and sent with matching requests.

  • Uses: Remembering preferences, carrying a session ID and supporting analytics.
  • Lifetime: A cookie can last for a browser session or persist until a configured expiry.
Response header · browser stores the value
Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Path=/; Max-Age=3600
Later request header · browser sends it back
Cookie: theme=dark

Path=/ applies across this host’s paths.

Max-Age=3600 sets a one-hour lifetime.

Set-Cookie and Cookie are HTTP headers, not response-body data. The browser stores cookies and sends them according to their scope and browser policy.

Cookies and Sessions

In a common server-side session design, the browser keeps an ID and the server keeps the login state.

  1. Browser1

    POST /login

    Send username
    and password

    Create session

    Verify credentials;

  3. Server → Browser3

    200 OK

Step 5 · Request with saved Cookies

Complete HTTP/1.1 GET request · no body
GET /profile HTTP/1.1
Host: lesson.example
Accept: application/json
Cookie: theme=dark; session_id=abc123

Cookie options

OptionMeaning
HttpOnlyPage JavaScript cannot read this cookie.
SecureSend the cookie over HTTPS.
SameSite=LaxRestrict when cross-site requests carry it.

Both values are in the Cookie request header, separated by a semicolon (;). This GET request has no body. The server uses session_id to find and validate the login session.

API, Endpoint, Routing and Handler

API
Application Programming Interface: a contract defining operations, inputs and outputs for software.
Endpoint
A specific API operation, identified here by an HTTP method + path.

Matching the request’s method and path to the code that handles the operation.

Example task: Retrieve the past year of historical prices for AAPL in the US market.

Example · historical prices
GET /api/history?id=AAPL%3AXNAS&range=1Y&market=US
HTTP methodGET
EndpointGET /api/history
Query inputsid range market

GET is the HTTP method; handleMarketApi(request) is the JavaScript handler function. Query values select the stock and range; the path selects the history operation.

Backend Development / Part 0222 / 50
PART 02 · FROM CLIENT TO SERVER

What Is a RESTful API?

A RESTful API applies REST architectural principles to interactions with resources.

REST means Representational State Transfer.

For an HTTP API, identify a resource with a URL and use standard HTTP methods to act on it.

OperationAction-oriented API · illustrativeResource-oriented HTTP API · illustrative
Read a stockPOST /api/getStockGET /api/stocks/AAPL
Create a stockPOST /api/createStockPOST /api/stocks
Change a stockPOST /api/updateStockPATCH /api/stocks/AAPL
Delete a stockPOST /api/deleteStockDELETE /api/stocks/AAPL

Without a shared resource interface, each operation can have its own endpoint name. Both designs can work; REST emphasizes a uniform interface. The left examples supply stock IDs and other inputs in their bodies.

Backend Development / Part 0223 / 50
PART 02 · FROM CLIENT TO SERVER

Designing a RESTful API

Representational State Transfer is an architectural style, not just a URL naming rule.

ResourceIllustrative operationMeaning
Stock collectionGET /api/stocksRead the collection
One stockGET /api/stocks/AAPLRead a stock representation
Historical pricesGET /api/stocks/AAPL/history?range=1yRead a related collection
A saved-stock entryPUT /api/watchlist/AAPLCreate or replace its saved state
A saved-stock entryDELETE /api/watchlist/AAPLRemove the association

Simplified REST-style design. REST also concerns constraints such as stateless interactions, a uniform interface and cacheability. Resource-oriented URLs alone do not establish full REST compliance.

PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

What Is Node.js?

Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser so a program can run on your operating system.

JavaScript leaves the browser.
What changes on the server?

Teaching Example · hello-node.mjs (run: node hello-node.mjs)
// Runs directly in your terminal — no browser tab neededimport { platform, arch } from 'node:os'; // Built-in OS info console.log('Node version:', process.version); // Installed Nodeconsole.log('Machine:', platform(), arch()); // OS & CPU typeconsole.log('Working folder:', process.cwd()); // Terminal dir
IN THE BROWSER

Frontend runtime

  • Provides document and window for buttons and charts.
  • Enforces browser security rules such as same-origin policies.
  • Stops running as soon as the user closes the tab.
IN NODE.JS

Backend runtime

  • Executes JavaScript directly on your OS using the V8 engine.
  • Provides node:http, node:fs and node:sqlite for servers and files.
  • Can stay running in the terminal to listen for requests.

Backend Development / Part 0326 / 50
PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

A Minimal HTTP Server

createServer registers a callback that runs every time a request arrives—not once at startup.

Teaching Example · minimal Node.js server
import { createServer } from 'node:http'; // Built-in HTTP module // Register a callback that wakes up on each browser visitconst server = createServer((req, res) => {  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }); // Headers  res.end(JSON.stringify({ ok: true, path: req.url })); // Send JSON}); server.listen(3000, '127.0.0.1'); // Stay awake on port 3000
01
Startup runs once

createServer stores your function and listen() binds port 3000.

02
Waiting costs almost nothing

When nobody clicks, the handler function is idle.

03
Request wakes the callback

Each browser visit invokes (req, res) => { ... } with fresh objects.

04
Reply completes the exchange

res.writeHead sets status and headers; res.end finishes the response.

Backend Development / Part 0327 / 50
PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

Receiving & Routing at the Door

A web server splits static webpage requests from /api/ calls, then routes each API endpoint.

Example · HTTP server entry
const maxRequestBytes = 16 * 1024; // Cap upload size at 16 KiBconst url = new URL(incoming.url, 'http://127.0.0.1'); // Parse URLif (url.pathname.startsWith('/api/')) { // Stage 1: API traffic  const body = await readBodyUpTo(incoming, maxRequestBytes); // Guard  const request = new Request(url, { method: incoming.method, body });  const response = await handleApi(request); // Stage 2: API route  outgoing.writeHead(response.status, Object.fromEntries(response.headers));  outgoing.end(Buffer.from(await response.arrayBuffer())); // Send reply  return;}const asset = assets.get(url.pathname); // Static file, or 404

Two-stage routing: the entry listener separates webpage files from /api/ calls, then handleApi(request) picks the matching endpoint handler.

01
Two paths on one port

Static paths read from assets; /api/* enters handleApi(request).

02
16 KiB payload limit

maxRequestBytes caps uploads before buffering, protecting server memory.

03
Request / Response adapter

Wraps incoming into a standard Request and writes response back to outgoing.

Example · inside handleApi(request) (API routing)
async function handleApi(request) {  const path = new URL(request.url).pathname; // Extract API path  if (path === '/api/stocks')    return json(listStocks()); // Stocks  if (path === '/api/history')   return json(getHistory(request)); // Chart  if (path === '/api/watchlist') return handleWatchlist(request); // Saved  return json({ error: 'Endpoint not found.' }, 404); // Fallback 404}
Backend Development / Part 0328 / 50
PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

Checking Inputs at the Gate

UI buttons only offer valid choices, yet anyone can send raw HTTP requests—the server must verify inputs.

Example · stock history input validation
const KEY_PATTERN = /^[0-9A-Z.]{1,20}:[A-Z0-9]{4}$/; // TICKER:MICconst RANGE_POINTS = { '5D': 5, '1M': 22, '3M': 66, '1Y': 252 };function parseStockId(id) { // Gate 1: validate ticker:exchange format  if (!KEY_PATTERN.test(id || '')) throw new ApiFault(400, 'Provide AAPL:XNAS.');  return id;}if (url.pathname === '/api/history') {  const id = parseStockId(url.searchParams.get('id')); // Verify ID  const range = url.searchParams.get('range') || '1M'; // Default 1M  if (!Object.hasOwn(RANGE_POINTS, range)) throw new ApiFault(400, 'Invalid range.'); // Gate 2  const stock = findStock(id); // Look up instrument record  if (!stock) throw new ApiFault(404, 'Stock not found.'); // Gate 3  return json({ range, points: loadHistory(stock, range) }); // Return JSON}
01
Gate 1 · Format check (400)

parseStockId() enforces ticker + 4-char exchange MIC (e.g. AAPL:XNAS).

02
Gate 2 · Allowed values (400)

RANGE_POINTS accepts only 5D, 1M, 3M, or 1Y—rejecting 10Y.

03
Gate 3 · Record exists (404)

Valid syntax is not enough: FAKE:XNAS passes regex yet returns 404.

Like a bank back office, the server never trusts client UI controls alone—external scripts can bypass dropdowns and call the URL directly.

Backend Development / Part 0329 / 50
PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

Handling Failures Cleanly

Structured error classes and a single try / catch turn predictable failures into safe JSON responses.

Example · centralized error handling
class ApiFault extends Error { // Error carrying an HTTP status  constructor(status, message) {    super(message); this.status = status;  }}try {  return await routeRequest(request); // Run normal route logic} catch (error) {  if (error instanceof ApiFault) // Known validation/client error    return json({ error: error.message }, error.status);  console.error('Unexpected error:', error); // Log privately  return json({ error: 'Service unavailable.' }, 500); // Safe reply}
StatusWhen the server returns itShown to client
400Bad ticker format, range, or JSONSpecific correction message
404Unknown stock or unknown endpointNot found message
405Wrong HTTP method (e.g., POST /api/history)Method error + Allow header
429Upstream provider rate limit reachedWait time + Retry-After
500Unexpected bug inside server codeGeneric message; details stay in server logs

Never send raw stack traces or internal code paths to browsers—log details privately with console.error and return a safe { error } object.

Backend Development / Part 0332 / 50
PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

Native Node.js vs. Web Frameworks

Frameworks like Express reduce boilerplate in large apps; native Node.js keeps every step visible.

Native Node.js · explicit routing
if (request.method !== 'GET') // Check HTTP method explicitly  return json({ error: 'Method not allowed.' }, 405);if (url.pathname === '/api/history') { // Match route path  const id = url.searchParams.get('id'); // Read ?id=...  const range = url.searchParams.get('range') || '1M'; // Default  return json({ id, range, points: loadHistory(id, range) });}
Express Framework · route helper
import express from 'express'; // Third-party web frameworkconst app = express();app.get('/api/history', (req, res) => { // GET + path together  const { id, range = '1M' } = req.query; // Query pre-parsed  const points = loadHistory(id, range); // Compute price bars  res.json({ id, range, points }); // Sets header & sends JSON});
AspectNative Node.jsExpress Framework
CapabilitiesFull HTTP routing, JSON, headers & errorsSame HTTP capabilities with helper methods
DependenciesZero external packages requiredRequires installing express via npm
Trade-offEvery step from URL to Response is visibleLess boilerplate when large teams share middleware
Backend Development / Part 0333 / 50
PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Work

Waiting synchronously blocks every other user; asynchronous I/O lets Node serve concurrently.

Synchronous (blocking wait)Student B waits for Student A’s network call
Student A
Handle A
Freeze & wait for market API (800 ms)
Reply A
Student B
Stuck waiting in queue…
Finally handle B
Asynchronous (non-blocking I/O)Node serves Student B while A’s API is in flight
Student A
Start A
External API working in background…
Resume & reply A
Student B
Handle B
Reply B
Single JavaScript thread

Node runs your JS code one step at a time—just like one bank teller handling requests.

Don’t stand waiting

Like giving a customer a buzzer at a café, start the slow network request and serve the next person.

Concurrency ≠ magic speed

Overlapping wait time keeps the server responsive, while heavy local CPU work still blocks the lane.

PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

Using async / await and fetch

await pauses only the current async function while other requests continue—protected by a timeout.

Example · fetching external market data
async function fetchMarketData(url, apiKey) { // Enables await  const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(7000); // 7s timeout stop-loss  try {    const response = await fetch(url, { // Yield while waiting      headers: { Authorization: apiKey }, // Send API credentials      signal, // Cancel fetch automatically if 7s passes    });    return await response.json(); // Parse response body as JSON  } catch {    if (signal.aborted) throw new ApiFault(504, 'Timed out.');    throw new ApiFault(502, 'Provider unreachable.'); // Network err  }}
01
async returns a Promise

A Promise represents a future result—either fulfilled data or a rejected error.

02
await yields cleanly

Suspends only this function while waiting on fetch, leaving Node free for other visitors.

03
AbortSignal.timeout sets a stop-loss

If an upstream provider stalls past 7 seconds, the request aborts and throws 504.

Notice try / catch works naturally with await: a failed network call or aborted timeout drops straight into catch.

Backend Development / Part 0335 / 50
PART 03 · BACKEND DEVELOPMENT WITH NODE.JS

Async Network vs. Sync SQLite

Writing await does not turn a synchronous call into non-blocking background work.

EXTERNAL NETWORK · ASYNC

Waiting on another server

Example · async fetch over Internet
// Network round trip (~100–1000 ms); yields JS threadconst response = await fetch(url, { signal }); // Non-blockingconst data = await response.json(); // Parse stream when ready
  • Yields the JavaScript thread while packets travel.
  • Essential for external market APIs and remote services.
LOCAL SQLITE · SYNCHRONOUS

Reading embedded local storage

Example · sync query via node:sqlite
import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite'; // Built-in SQLiteconst stmt = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM stocks WHERE id = ?'); // Compilereturn stmt.get(id); // Runs synchronously in µs; no await
  • Runs directly on the main thread in microseconds.
  • No await needed—and adding await would not make it async.

A backend can mix both intentionally: external HTTP requests use async fetch, while tiny local SQLite lookups run synchronously.

How do we keep a saved list
after the backend restarts?

IN MEMORY

JavaScript variables / Map

Useful while this process runs.

The in-memory collection is lost when that process stops.

ON DISK

A file-backed database

PART 04 · DATABASES WITH SQLITE

SQLite and SQL

SQLite is a database engine; SQL is the language used to describe database operations.

SQLite · the engine

  • An embedded, relational database engine.
  • The application uses a library to read and write a database file.
  • A separate database server process is not required.

SQL · the language

  • Structured Query Language.
  • Statements describe what to read or change.
  • Examples: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
BrowserHTTP request
→
Node.js processApplication + SQLite engine
→
Database filePersistent records
A SQL statement
SELECT symbol, price FROM stocks;

The web application still has a backend server. SQLite removes the need for a separate database server, not the application server.

PART 04 · DATABASES WITH SQLITE

Defining a Table

A schema describes columns, their accepted values and the rules for records.

Classroom subset · CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE classroom_stocks (
  source TEXT NOT NULL,
  id TEXT NOT NULL,
  symbol TEXT NOT NULL,
  market TEXT NOT NULL,
  price REAL,
  PRIMARY KEY (source, id)
) STRICT;

Read the definition

Declaration / valueMeaning
TEXTText values
INTEGERInteger values
REALFloating-point values
NULLA missing value; not the text "null"
  • NOT NULL: a value is required.
  • PRIMARY KEY: identifies a row uniquely.
  • STRICT: enforce the declared types in this table.

price may be NULL here because it is not declared NOT NULL. Ordinary SQLite tables use flexible typing; this example uses STRICT, like the project.

Reading Data with SELECT

Choose columns, choose a table, then restrict which records are returned.

SELECT · FROM · WHERE
SELECT symbol, price
FROM stocks
WHERE source = 'demo' AND market = 'US'
  AND price >= 180;

Meaning

  • SELECT: return symbol and price.
  • FROM: read the stocks table.
  • WHERE: keep demo US stocks priced at least 180.

Query result · fictional classroom data

symbolprice
AAPL190.0
MSFT420.0

SELECT returns rows without changing the stored records. Without ORDER BY, the result order is not guaranteed.

Backend Development / Part 0441 / 50
PART 04 · DATABASES WITH SQLITE

Sorting and Limiting Results

ORDER BY defines the order; LIMIT and OFFSET select a portion of that ordered result.

The two highest classroom US prices
SELECT symbol, price
FROM stocks
WHERE source = 'demo' AND market = 'US'
ORDER BY price DESC, symbol ASC
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 0;

Useful clauses

  • DESC: descending; ASC: ascending.
  • LIMIT 2: return at most two rows.
  • OFFSET 0: skip no rows; change to 2 for the next page.

Query result · fictional classroom data

symbolprice
MSFT420.0
AAPL190.0

Use a stable ordering for pagination. The symbol is a tie-breaker when prices are equal; comparisons here stay within the same market.

PART 04 · DATABASES WITH SQLITE

Foreign Keys: Keeping References Valid

A foreign key requires a referenced record to exist in another table.

Foreign key: columns that reference a primary or unique key in another table.

watchlistReferencing table

user_idregionstock_id
AliceUSAAPL
AliceJP7203
BobCN600036
Must reference(region, stock_id)→(region, id)

stocksPRIMARY KEY (region, id)

regionidname
USAAPLApple
JP7203Toyota
CN600036CMB
Declare the rule on watchlist
CREATE TABLE watchlist (
  user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  region TEXT NOT NULL,
  stock_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (region, stock_id)
    REFERENCES stocks(region, id)
);

Both values must match

Accepted: JP / 7203
Toyota exists with this region and ID.

Rejected: US / 7203
No stock has this pair of values.

REFERENCES stocks(region, id)
names the target table and columns.

SQLite enforcement: enable PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; for each connection.

Run the valid insert, then change JP to US to trigger an error.

PART 04 · DATABASES WITH SQLITE

Using SQLite from Node.js

JavaScript calls the database API; SQL describes the operation inside the database.

Node.js · read with get() and write with run()
import { DatabaseSync } from 'node:sqlite';
const db = new DatabaseSync('classroom.sqlite');
const query = db.prepare(`
  SELECT symbol, price FROM stocks
  WHERE source = 'demo' AND id = ?
`);
const stock = query.get('AAPL:XNAS');
const update = db.prepare(`
  UPDATE stocks SET price = ?
  WHERE source = 'demo' AND id = ?
`);
const info = update.run(190, 'AAPL:XNAS');
console.log(stock, info);
db.close();

The important calls

CallPurpose
new DatabaseSync(...)Open a database connection.
prepare(sql)Compile a statement.
get(...)Read the first matching row.
all(...)Read all result rows.
run(...)Execute a write statement.

get → { symbol: "AAPL", price: 190 }
run → { changes: 1, ... }

Backend Development / Part 0447 / 50
PART 04 · DATABASES WITH SQLITE

Transactions

Group related database changes so that they commit together or are rolled back together.

BEGINStart the transaction
→
Write stockEnsure its record exists
→
Write watchlistSave its reference
→
COMMIT / ROLLBACKKeep or undo the writes
The transaction boundary
BEGIN IMMEDIATE;
INSERT INTO stocks (...) VALUES (...);
INSERT INTO watchlist (...) VALUES (...);
COMMIT; -- or ROLLBACK;

Read the intent

  • COMMIT: make the transaction’s changes permanent.
  • ROLLBACK: undo its uncommitted changes.
  • The project wraps related writes in a transaction.
  • Its JavaScript error handler performs rollback on failure.

In the editor, switch the COMMIT statement to ROLLBACK. AMZN then disappears from the resulting saved list; the original saved records remain.

Backend Development / Part 0448 / 50
PART 04 · DATABASES WITH SQLITE

Complete SQLite Workflow: Schema to CRUD

Create one fully constrained table, then run Create, Read, Update and Delete in one example.

1. Comprehensive CREATE TABLE · constraints
CREATE TABLE student_holdings (
  holding_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  source TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'demo',
  stock_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  shares INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (shares > 0),
  note TEXT DEFAULT '',
  FOREIGN KEY (source, stock_id)
    REFERENCES stocks(source, id),
  UNIQUE (source, stock_id)
) STRICT;
  • PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT generates holding_id (1, 2...); UNIQUE blocks duplicate stocks.
  • NOT NULL, DEFAULT, CHECK (shares > 0), FOREIGN KEY and STRICT guard invalid rows.
2. Full CRUD · INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE
-- C · Create (uses DEFAULT 'demo')
INSERT INTO student_holdings (stock_id, shares, note) VALUES
  ('AAPL:XNAS', 10, 'Core'), ('MSFT:XNAS', 5, 'Cloud');
-- R · Read (JOIN stocks + sort)
SELECT h.holding_id, s.symbol, h.shares, s.price
FROM student_holdings AS h
JOIN stocks AS s ON s.source = h.source AND s.id = h.stock_id
ORDER BY h.shares DESC;
-- U · Update
UPDATE student_holdings SET shares = 15 WHERE stock_id = 'AAPL:XNAS';
-- D · Delete & check final state
DELETE FROM student_holdings WHERE stock_id = 'MSFT:XNAS';
SELECT holding_id, stock_id, shares, note FROM student_holdings;

Final row after CRUD: { holding_id: 1, stock_id: "AAPL:XNAS", shares: 15 }

Try inserting shares = 0 (triggers CHECK), repeating AAPL:XNAS (UNIQUE), or saving FAKE:XNAS (FOREIGN KEY) in the SQL lab.

Other Relational Databases

Tables, keys, joins and transactions also appear in server-based relational database systems.

DatabaseRecognizable featuresWhat transfers from SQLite
MySQLA server-based relational DB; InnoDB supports transactions.Tables, SQL queries, keys and joins.
PostgreSQLAn extensible object-relational DB with rich data types.Relational modeling and transactional work.
SQL ServerMicrosoft’s relational DB; applications use T-SQL.SQL fundamentals and integrity constraints.
Oracle DatabaseA multiuser database with SQL and PL/SQL.Schema design, joins and transactions.
SQLiteApplication + engine → local file
Server-based DBApplication → driver / connection → database server

Deployment, administration and SQL dialects differ. Moving databases still requires reviewing data types, syntax and application connection code.

Non-Relational Databases

NoSQL covers several data models with different ways to organize and access information.

ModelExampleShape of the dataIllustrative use
DocumentMongoDBJSON-like documents with fields and arrays.Product details or flexible application records.
Key–valueRedisKeys pointing to values / data structures.Cached quotes, counters or session data.
Wide-columnApache CassandraPartitioned records organized for known queries.Large event streams or time-oriented workloads.
GraphNeo4jNodes connected by relationships.Connections among people, companies or assets.
Document{ symbol: "AAPL", ... }
Key–valuequote:AAPL → 190
GraphInvestor → FOLLOWS → Stock

Choose for the data model and access patterns. NoSQL does not mean “no schema” or “no transactions”; relational databases can also support JSON.
